summary: Describes an LDAPv3 control that lets a client ask a directory server to return search results in pages instead of all at once. The client fetches one chunk at a time and asks for the next, which keeps large searches manageable. This is an informational memo, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo adds a control to the LDAP directory protocol so that a client can ask for search results in batches. The client says how many entries it wants and sends back a token the server gave it, and the server uses that token to work out where to carry on from. The client can stop at any point and pick the search up again later.

subtitle: An LDAP control that lets a client fetch a large search result set one page at a time instead of all at once.

tldr.problem: A directory search can match far more entries than a client can hold, and on a slow link the server has to send them all before the client sees anything. LDAP has no standard way to ask for a search result in pieces.
tldr.mechanism: The control carries a page size and a cookie. The client sends a search request with the size it wants and an empty cookie; the server returns that many entries and a new cookie, and the client sends the cookie back to fetch the next page.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and defines a protocol extension rather than a standard. It also warns that a client can use the control to learn how many entries match a filter before receiving any of them, which servers with access control checks must handle.

today: RFC 2696 is an Informational memo from September 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines an extension to the LDAPv3 protocol defined in RFC 2251 rather than a standard in its own right.

sections.title: The Control
sections.content:
RFC 2696 describes an LDAPv3 control extension for simple paging of search results. The control lets a client control the rate at which an LDAP server returns the results of a search operation. It may be useful when the LDAP client has limited resources and cannot process the entire result set from a given query, or when the client is connected over a low-bandwidth connection. Other operations on the result set are not defined, and the extension is not designed to provide more sophisticated result set management.

The control is included in the searchRequest and searchResultDone messages, as part of the controls field of the LDAPMessage. Its structure is a SEQUENCE of three parts: a control type, whose value is the object identifier 1.2.840.113556.1.4.319; a criticality flag, a BOOLEAN that defaults to false; and a control value.

The control value is an octet string wrapping the BER-encoded version of a SEQUENCE with two fields. The size field is an integer with the range 0 to maxInt: on the request it carries the page size asked for by the client, and on the response it carries the server's estimate of the result set size. The cookie field is an octet string, empty on the first request and carrying the server's token on later ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The control is a small structure added to two of LDAP's messages. It holds a number, which is the page size the client wants, and a token, which is empty on the first request. The server fills the number in with its own estimate of how many entries match, and fills the token in with something the client must send back to continue.

sections.title: Client-Server Interaction
sections.content:
A client that needs to control the rate at which results are returned MAY specify on the searchRequest a paged results control with the size set to the desired page size and the cookie set to the zero-length string. The page size MAY be greater than zero and less than the size limit value specified in the request.

If the page size is greater than or equal to the size limit, the server should ignore the control, because the request can then be satisfied in a single page. If the server does not support the control, it MUST return an error of unsupportedCriticalExtension if the client requested it as critical, and otherwise the server SHOULD ignore the control.

Each time the server returns a set of results, it includes the control in the searchResultDone message. The size MAY be set to the server's estimate of the total number of entries in the entire result set, and a server that cannot provide such an estimate MAY set it to zero. The cookie MUST be set to an empty value if there are no more entries to return, that is, if the page just returned was the last, and otherwise it is an octet string of the server's choosing, used to resume the search.

The client MUST consider the cookie to be an opaque structure and make no assumptions about its internal organization or value. When it wants more entries, it MUST send a searchRequest with all values identical to the initial request, except for the messageID, the cookie, and optionally a modified page size. The cookie MUST be the octet string from the last searchResultDone response. Returning cookies from earlier responses is undefined, because the server implementation may restrict cookies from being reused.

The exchange continues until the client has retrieved all the results, at which point the cookie in the searchResultDone field is empty, or until the client abandons the search sequence. Once the paged search sequence has been completed, the cookie is no longer valid and MUST NOT be used. A sequence of paged search requests is abandoned by sending a search request with the size set to zero and the cookie set to the last cookie returned by the server. A client MAY use the LDAP Abandon operation to abandon one paged search request in progress, but this is discouraged because it MAY invalidate the client's cookie.

If the server cannot resume a paged search operation for a client, it SHOULD return the appropriate error in a searchResultDone entry, and both client and server should then assume the paged result set is closed and no longer resumable. A client may have any number of outstanding search requests pending, any of which may have used the control. A server that requires a limit on the number of outstanding paged search requests from a given client MAY either return unwillingToPerform when the client attempts to create a new one, or age out an older result set, in which case it SHOULD return unwilling to perform if the client tries to resume the aged-out search.

A client may safely assume that all entries satisfying a given search query are returned once and only once during the set of requests and responses needed to enumerate the entire result set, unless the result set for that query has changed since the request that started the sequence was processed. In that case the client may receive a given entry multiple times, and may not receive all the entries matching the criteria.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends the search with a page size. The server sends back that many entries plus a token, and the client sends the token back with an otherwise identical search to get the next page. The server chooses the token and the client must treat it as an opaque string it cannot inspect or modify. When the last page has been sent the token is empty, and the client must not send an empty or old token again because the server may have forgotten it.

sections.title: The Example Exchange
sections.content:
The memo's example shows a client doing a search with a page size limit of 3, against a result set of 5 entries. Lines beginning with C are requests sent from the client to the server, lines beginning with S are responses sent from the server to the client, and lines beginning with two dashes are explanatory comments.

The client first sends a search request with a paged results control of (3, an empty cookie). The server responds with three search result entries, then a searchResultDone carrying a paged results control of (5, an opaque token). The 5 is the server's indication of the total number of entries in the search result, and the opaque token is what the client must send back when it wants the next page.

The client then sends an identical search request, except for the message id, carrying the opaque token and asking for the next page. The server responds with two more entries and a searchResultDone with a paged results control of (5, an empty cookie), which says there are no more entries to return.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example the client asks for three entries at a time from a result set of five. The first reply brings three entries and a token. The client sends the token back and gets the last two entries, this time with an empty token, which means the search is over.

sections.title: Relationship to X.500
sections.content: For LDAP servers providing a front end to X.500 directories, the paged results control defined in this document may be mapped directly onto the X.500 PagedResultsRequest. The size parameter may be mapped onto pageSize, and the cookie parameter may be mapped onto queryReference. The sortKeys and reverse fields of the X.500 PagedResultsRequest are excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: For a directory server that also speaks the older X.500 protocol, the two mechanisms line up field for field: the page size maps to pageSize and the token maps to queryReference. Only the sorting options of the X.500 version have no equivalent here.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Server implementors should consider the resources used when clients send searches with the simple paged control, to ensure that a client's misuse of the control does not lock out other legitimate operations. Server implementations may enforce an overriding size limit, to prevent the retrieval of large portions of a publicly accessible directory.

The memo also notes a side effect of the design. Clients can, using this control, determine how many entries match a particular filter before the entries are returned to the client. This may require special processing in servers which perform access control checks on entries, to determine whether the existence of the entry can be disclosed to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: Two points matter for a server operator. A client can use paging to make the server work hard, so the server should keep a limit on how much work one client can ask for. And the size the server reports back is a count of matching entries, which can reveal that an entry exists even when the client is not allowed to read it, so a server that filters entries by access rights has to think about that before it reports a count.
